In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], the '''flower snarks''' form an infinite family of [[snark (graph theory)|snark]]s introduced by [[Rufus Isaacs (game theorist)|Rufus Isaacs]] in 1975.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Isaacs |first=R. |title=Infinite Families of Nontrivial Trivalent Graphs Which Are Not Tait Colorable |journal=Amer. Math. Monthly |volume=82 |pages=221–239 |year=1975 |issue=3 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1975.11993805 |jstor=2319844}}</ref>

As snarks, the flower snarks are [[connectivity (graph theory)|connected]], [[bridge (graph theory)|bridge]]less [[cubic graph|cubic]] [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]s with [[chromatic index]] equal to 4. The flower snarks are [[planar graph|non-planar]] and [[Hamiltonian graph|non-Hamiltonian]], though they are [[1-planar_graph|1-planar]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Pupyrev | first = Sergey
 | editor-first1 = Vida | editor-last1 = Dujmović | editor-first2 = Fabrizio | editor-last2 = Montecchiani
 | contribution = OOPS: Optimized One-Planarity Solver via SAT
 | title = Proc. 33rd International Symposium on Graph Drawing and Network Visualization (GD 2025)
 | series = Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs)
 | year = 2025 | volume = 357 | pages = 14:1–14:19
 | doi = 10.4230/LIPIcs.GD.2025.14
 | isbn = 978-3-95977-403-1 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> 
The flower snarks  J<sub>5</sub> and J<sub>7</sub> have [[book thickness]] 3 and [[queue number]] 2.<ref>Wolz, Jessica; ''Engineering Linear Layouts with SAT.'' Master Thesis, University of Tübingen, 2018</ref>

==Construction==
The flower snark J<sub>''n''</sub> can be constructed with the following process :
* Build ''n'' copies of the [[star graph]] on 4 [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]]. Denote the central vertex of each star A<sub>''i''</sub> and the outer vertices B<sub>''i''</sub>, C<sub>''i''</sub> and D<sub>''i''</sub>. This results in a disconnected graph on 4''n'' vertices with 3''n'' edges (A<sub>''i''</sub> − B<sub>''i''</sub>, A<sub>''i''</sub> − C<sub>''i''</sub> and A<sub>''i''</sub> − D<sub>''i''</sub> for 1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''n'').
* Construct the ''n''-cycle (B<sub>1</sub>... B<sub>''n''</sub>). This adds ''n'' edges.
* Finally construct the 2''n''-cycle (C<sub>1</sub>... C<sub>''n''</sub>D<sub>1</sub>... D<sub>''n''</sub>). This adds ''2n'' edges.

By construction, the Flower snark J<sub>''n''</sub> is a cubic graph with 4''n'' vertices and 6''n'' edges.  For it to have the required properties, ''n'' should be [[parity (mathematics)|odd]].

==Special cases==
The name flower snark is sometimes used for J<sub>5</sub>, a flower snark with 20 vertices and 30 edges.<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Flower Snark|urlname=FlowerSnark}}</ref> It is one of 6 snarks on 20 vertices {{OEIS|id=A130315}}. The flower snark J<sub>5</sub> is [[hypohamiltonian graph|hypohamiltonian]].<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Hypohamiltonian Graph|urlname=HypohamiltonianGraph}}</ref>

J<sub>3</sub> is a trivial variation of the [[Petersen graph]] formed by replacing one of its vertices by a triangle. This graph is also known as the [[Tietze's graph]].<ref>{{citation|first1=L.|last1=Clark|first2=R.|last2=Entringer|title=Smallest maximally nonhamiltonian graphs|journal=Periodica Mathematica Hungarica|volume=14|issue=1|year=1983|pages=57–68|doi=10.1007/BF02023582}}.</ref> In order to avoid trivial cases, snarks are generally restricted to have [[girth (graph theory)|girth]] at least 5. With that restriction, J<sub>3</sub> is not a snark.
